en: The Procedure for Recollecting the Eightfold Pastimes of Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa:
Having thus meditated upon Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa upon the lotus,
one should then perform service appropriate for the eight times [of the day] with a perfected body.
There, by the command of the assembly of gurus, one should worship Rādhikā and Hari.
Then, having performed the external worship, as well as the water for the feet and the respectful offering (arghya) in due order,
the practitioner, following the sequence after service according to the prescribed rite,
should unweariedly recite the mantras whose mouths consist of thirty-two syllables.
First, one should recite the great mantra consisting of ten syllables;
after that, the mantra of Śrī Rādhikā; and then the Gāyatrī and the Kāmikī mantras.
Then one should recite the couple-mantra (yugala-mantra) which bestows the site of the rāsa dance;
then one should recite the mantras of the eight female companions (sakhīs) in their proper order;
and then one should recite the respective mantras of the eight Mañjarīs in sequence.
The *Aṣṭakālīyasūtra* states as follows: "Evening, morning, forenoon, midday, afternoon, evening, dusk, and night—these are the eight times in their proper order. (RKK 5)
Both midday and midnight are traditionally held to measure six muhūrtas;
the others, beginning with the end of night, should be known to measure three muhūrtas each.
Regarding service to them by one who has attained a perfected body (*siddha-deha*), it is stated in the *Sanat-kumāra-saṃhitā*:
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, O Guru, everything that was asked by you has been explained."
Now I wish to hear the unsurpassed path of passion.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"Well asked by you, O Brahmin, who desire the welfare of all the worlds!
I shall speak even the secret; listen as it is told by me."
Those who consider themselves the wives of others, as well as his own beloveds,
delight their own dear one with an exceedingly intense emotion.
There, in their midst, one should contemplate oneself as a charming young woman,
endowed with beauty and youth, possessing the form of a maiden.
She was skilled in various arts and crafts and suited to Kṛṣṇa’s enjoyments;
yet, even when solicited by Kṛṣṇa, she remained averse to such pleasures.
She is an eternal follower of Rādhikā, ever devoted to her service,
and she directs even greater love toward Rādhikā than toward Kṛṣṇa himself.
Day by day, with joyful effort, she brought about their union;
she was exceedingly contented by the abundance of savoring the bliss of serving them.
Having thus reflected upon oneself, one should perform service there,
beginning from the Brāhma-muhūrta until the great night of deep sleep.
Śrī Nārada said:
I wish to hear, according to the truth, the pastimes of Hari performed here;
for how can Hari be served in the mind by those who do not know his pastimes?
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
"O Nārada, I do not know that pastime of Hari in its true essence.
Go to Goddess Vṛndā; she will describe that pastime to you."
Not far from this place, near the Keśī-tīrtha,
she dwells surrounded by her friends as an attendant of Govinda.
Śrī Sanatkumāra said: Having been addressed thus, that best of sages, Nārada, circumambulated his guru and bowed to him again and again, and then departed for the abode of Vṛndāvana.
Vṛndā, too, seeing Nārada and bowing down to him again and again, spoke to that best of sages: "How is it that you have come here?"
Śrī Nārada said:
O beautiful one, I wish to learn from you the daily conduct of Hari;
therefore, tell it to me from the beginning, if I am worthy, O auspicious lady.
Śrī Vṛndādevī said: O Nārada, you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa; I shall tell you a secret.
This great mystery, more secret than the secret, must certainly not be disclosed by you.
Now, regarding the service at the end of the night: in the midst of beautiful Vṛndāvana, adorned with fifty groves,
within a bower of wish-fulfilling trees, in a house made of divine jewels.
Though they remained on their bed, fast asleep and locked in a firm embrace with one another,
they were awakened later by birds acting upon my command.
Fearing the breaking of that embrace during a firm embrace,
the two did not have the slightest thought of rising from the bed.
Then, repeatedly awakened by flocks of śārikas, parrots,
and other birds with various verses, the two rose from their own bed.
Then, seeing the two friends seated joyfully upon the couch,
their attendants entered and performed for them the services appropriate to that occasion.
And again, at the words of Śārikā, they both rose from their own bed and went to their respective abodes, agitated by mutual fear and longing.
Thus concludes the service at the end of the night;
now follows the morning service:
having been awakened by his mother in the morning, he rises quickly from his bed.
Having used his tooth-stick, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva, [performed his ablutions].
Permitted by his mother, he went to the cowshed eager to milk;
Rādhā too was awakened from her bed by her elderly female companions.
Having risen and used the tooth-stick and so forth, one should perform anointing;
then, having gone to the bathing altar, she is bathed by Lalitā and the others.
She should go to the dressing room there, where her female companions adorn her with various divine ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then, her own kinsmen, having earnestly entreated her mother-in-law,
quickly summoned Yaśodā along with her friend to cook for her.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Goddess, how was she summoned by Yaśodā for the sake of cooking,
even though there were other cooks present, headed by Rohiṇī?
Śrī Vṛndā said: "In the past, I heard from the mouth of Kātyāyanī that a boon had been granted to her by the great sage Durvāsas himself."
O Goddess, whatever food you cook shall, by my grace, be sweet, delicious,
rivaling nectar, and likewise bestow long life upon the eater.
Thus Yaśodā, who was deeply affectionate toward her son, would constantly call out to her,
"May my son be long-lived," because she was so devoted to him and fond of sweet things.
Permitted by her mother-in-law, she too, joyful and accompanied by a circle of her friends, would go to Nanda’s house; having arrived there, she prepares the food.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having milked some cows himself and having others milked by people,
returns to his own home surrounded by his friends at his father's command.
Having had an oil massage and a rubbing performed by servants, he was joyfully bathed;
wearing washed garments, adorned with garlands, his body anointed with sandalwood paste.
With hair tied in two tufts, [he is] radiant upon his neck and forehead;
he is adorned with a forehead mark (tilaka) in the shape of a moon shimmering upon his brow.
His hands are radiant with bracelets, armlets, upper-arm ornaments, and jeweled seals;
his chest gleams with a pearl necklace, and he wears earrings shaped like sea-monsters.
Repeatedly called by his mother, he should enter the dining hall,
holding his mother’s hand and following in the footsteps of Baladeva.
Having eaten various foods together with his mother and surrounded by his friends,
he amused them with diverse remarks while being amused by them in turn.
Having eaten in this manner and likewise sipped water for purification, he should rest for a moment upon a divine couch,
chewing the betel-leaf provided by his servants as they distribute it.
Rādhā too, seeing the joy of the meal and summoned by Yaśodā,
ate the food while surrounded by her friends, Lalitā and others, filled with bashfulness.
Thus concludes the morning service;
now follows the forenoon service:
Kṛṣṇa, wearing the attire of a cowherd, is preceded by a herd of cows.
He was followed along the path with affection by all the people residing in Vraja.
Having bowed to his father and mother with a sidelong glance, and having appropriately bid farewell to his circle of beloved ones and others, he should depart for the forest.
Having entered the forest and played with his friends for a moment,
he then deceived them all and departed accompanied by two or three dear companions.
Eager to see his beloved, he went to the rendezvous out of impetuosity;
she too, seeing that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the forest, arrived at the house.
Under the pretext of worshipping the sun and other deities, and by the guise of gathering flowers and such,
he deceives his teachers and goes to the forest out of a desire for union with his beloved.
Thus ends the service of the forenoon; now follows the service of midday:
having thus met with great effort, the two of them, surrounded by their own retinues, [proceeded].
There, in that forest, they sported joyfully with various kinds of dwellings.
In one place, Hari was rocked by his friends while mounted on a swing;
in another, his flute slipped from his hand as it was stolen by his beloved.
Searching [for her], he was reproached and deceived by his groups of beloved women;
laughed at in many ways by them, he stands as if his own wealth has been stolen.
Having entered with joy a certain forest grove graced by the spring season,
[he sprinkled it] with sandalwood water and waters mixed with saffron and other fragrances.
Even with the mud released from the water-jets discharged by the machines, those two splashed each other;
likewise their friends splashed them, and they in turn splashed those friends again.
Likewise, O twice-born one, as the other seasons arrived, they sported with their retinues in the forest groves, enjoying various diversions appropriate for each particular time.
O best of sages, having reached the foot of a tree somewhere while fatigued,
they sat upon a divine seat and partook of honey-wine.
Then, intoxicated by the honey [of wine], their eyes closed in sleep,
they grasped each other's hands, falling under the sway of the arrows of Love.
Desirous of sport, they entered the grove with their lotus-feet stumbling on the path,
like a male and female elephant playing there as leaders of their herd.
Her friends as well, intoxicated by honey and their eyes closed in sleep,
all dissolved away within the clusters of groves on every side.
Though Kṛṣṇa is one, the omnipresent Lord can simultaneously go into the presence of all his beloveds, moving repeatedly around them with individual forms.
Having delighted them all like a lordly elephant with his female elephants,
he should then go to the lake together with his beloved and those women.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Vṛndā, please dispel my doubt as to how the manifestation of the Lord’s sovereignty occurred during the sweet pastimes of the son of Śrī Nanda.
Śrī Vṛndā said:
O sage, within the sweetness of Lord Hari there exists a power of divine play (līlā-śakti) perceived by the vision [of the devotees];
separated from that [transcendental form] by that power, Hari sports together with the gopīs.
"He himself delights with his own form together with Rādhā"—
such is the power of Hari's sweet pastimes, not of his lordship.
Then, having played together there with mutual splashing of water, the two of them, along with their attendants,
were adorned with garments, garlands, sandalwood paste, and divine ornaments.
Right there, on the shore of that lake, in a house made of divine jewels,
you shall eat fruits and roots prepared by me alone.
But Hari, having first eaten what was served by his beloved and attended to by two or three [attendants], would go to the bed fashioned of flowers.
There, being served by those women with betel leaves, fans, and the massaging of his feet,
he was greatly delighted while remembering his beloved.
Then, even while Hari was asleep, Śrī Rādhā, her heart joyful and her mind delighted, ate the remnants given by her beloved along with her companions.
Having eaten just a little from that, she should go to her bedchamber,
like a female cakora bird to see the moon, to behold the lotus-face of her beloved.
The betel-chewing offered to him by the women there he partakes of, while his beloveds divide the remaining portions among themselves.
Kṛṣṇa, too, desiring to hear their private conversation, remained covered by his cloth; though wide awake, he appeared as if asleep.
Having exchanged for a moment playful jests among themselves concerning their beloved,
they perceived Hari’s feigned sleep through some inference.
Reflecting and gazing at one another’s faces with their eyes, they seemed as if paralyzed by shame; for a moment, they said nothing at all.
Then, in an instant, they removed the garment from his body and laughed at him, joking, "Well done! You have fallen fast asleep."
Thus, O best of sages, those two, sporting with their attendants through various jests, experienced for a moment the pleasure of sleep.
Having joyfully seated themselves upon a spacious, divine throne together with their retinues,
they staked against one another necklaces, kisses, embraces, and garments.
Playing at dice out of love, preceded by playful banter,
he falsely said "I have won" even though he had been defeated by his beloved.
When she set about seizing his necklaces and other ornaments, he was struck by her;
thus struck by her, Kṛṣṇa was hit with her ear-lotuses and lotuses.
With a dejected face, like one who has lost his wealth, Nārada said:
"O Goddess, I have been defeated by you; let that which was staked be taken."
Saying, "I have given you kisses and so forth," he acted accordingly;
yet he did so only to observe the knitting of her eyebrows and to hear her words of reproach.
Then, having heard the mutual verbal dispute between the partridges and the parrots,
he wished to depart from that place and go toward his home.
Kṛṣṇa, having taken leave of his beloved, should go toward the cows;
she, however, should go to the house of the Sun, accompanied by a circle of her female friends.
Having gone some distance from there and turned back again, Hari,
assuming the guise of a brahmin, proceeds toward the house of Sūrya.
There, at the request of her female companions, she should worship the Sun with improvised Vedic hymns that are infused with mockery and jesting.
Then those wise women, having recognized their beloved, were submerged in an ocean of bliss; they knew neither themselves nor anyone else.
Having thus spent two and a half watches of the night with him in various dwellings, they returned to their homes; and Kṛṣṇa went to the cow-pen.
Thus concludes the midday service;
now follows the afternoon service:
Kṛṣṇa, having gathered his friends together, took the cows from all sides.
He comes to Vraja, drawing [the cows] with the sounds of his flute held upwards.
Then Nanda and all the others, having heard the sound of Hari’s flute and seeing the expanse of the sky covered by clouds of dust from the cows, [were filled with joy].
Having abandoned all activities, even women, children,
and others go toward Kṛṣṇa, eager for the sight of him.
Rādhikā also, having returned home, bathed, and adorned herself, prepared various ingredients for her beloved’s enjoyment; then,
accompanied by a circle of her friends, she went forth, eager to see her beloved.
On the royal road at the gate of Vraja, where all the inhabitants of Vraja were gathered,
Kṛṣṇa also approached them and greeted them duly, one after another.
By means of sights or touches, or by glances preceded by smiles,
[he honored] the elder cowherds with physical prostrations as well as verbal salutations.
O Nārada, with prostrations of the eight limbs they honored their parents,
and likewise their beloved wives with a modesty indicated by the mere corners of their eyes.
Thus honored by those cowherds according to their respective merits,
he entered the cow-pen and the cattle on all sides.
Requested by his parents, he goes to his own home together with his brother;
having bathed, drunk, and likewise eaten something, and being permitted by his mother,
he goes again to the cow-pen, desiring to milk the cows' milk.
Thus concludes the afternoon service;
now follows the evening service— having milked some cows, having caused others to be milked, and having given drink to some.
He goes home together with his father, followed by hundreds of milk-carrying attendants.
There too, together with hosts of mothers, their sons, and armies,
he partakes of various kinds of food, such as things to be chewed and sucked.
Thus concludes the evening service; now follows the twilight (pradoṣa) service—
indeed, at that very time, even Rādhā, prior to her mother’s request, [performs it].
Cooked foods are sent to his residence by means of her female companions.
Praising those [offerings], the king, having eaten them together with his father and other elders,
should proceed to the assembly hall, which is frequented by bards and other attendants.
The friends who had gathered there took cooked foods,
and Yaśodā gave them many more in turn.
There, her friend gave her the remnants of Kṛṣṇa's meal in private;
then, having gathered all of it together, she presented it to Rādhikā.
Having eaten, she too, accompanied by her circle of friends, should remain adorned by those friends in that same sequence, filled with joy, in order to go forth to meet him.
By means of this [message], a certain female friend was dispatched from here to there;
she, in turn, was sent by her to the vicinity of the Yamunā.
In this bower of wish-fulfilling trees, within a mansion made of divine jewels,
she goes accompanied by her friends, dressed in attire suitable for the white and black nights.
Kṛṣṇa, too, having seen various wonders there,
and having heard charming poems as well as songs, was filled with curiosity.
Having gratified them with wealth, grain, and other gifts according to the prescribed rites,
and being summoned by his mother and the people, he goes to his bedchamber.
Once the mother has departed and [the son] has been fed, he should then go from the house to meet his beloved at the appointed place, remaining unobserved.
Thus ends the practice of the evening;
now follows the practice of the night—
both of these being practiced here together as they sport within the forest groves.
With various kinds of dwellings, preceded by laughter, dance, and song.
Having spent two and a half watches of the night dwelling in this manner, those two,
desiring sleep, entered the bower unobserved by five or six people.
On a delightful pleasure-couch strewn with flowers from which the stalks had been removed,
let them remain asleep there, attended by their beloved female companions.
Thus ends the service performed at night.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Lord, I desire to hear [the account] of the son of the King of Vraja."
Together with Rādhā, [experience] the divine nectar in Vṛndāvana, which is exclusively [for her].
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall speak of the pure rasa of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa;
it is most secret and supremely noble, and indeed must not be told to anyone.
O sage, in order to experience the exclusive savor of rasa, I meditated upon the prince of Vraja for a long time in Vṛndāvana.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with me, bestowed upon me the two unsurpassed mantras known as the "Couple," which are overflowing with His own radiant rasa.
Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to me, his own disciple:
"I shall tell you my own essence; listen now, for it is beyond the reach of Brahmā and the other gods."
The son of the King of Vraja, dwelling in the forest of Vṛndāvana as the most perfect one,
whose sixteen digits are complete, eternally performs his pastimes.
Vāsudeva, the most perfect, dwelling in the city of Mathurā,
always sports there, endowed with fifteen digits.
But that Pūrṇa, the lord of Dvārakā,
dwelling in Dvāravatī and endowed with the fourteen arts, remains ever engaged in his activities.
By one part and by two parts, the Lords of Mathurā and Dvārakā possess forms that are complete in their respective positions and aesthetic flavors, O Lord of Vṛndāvana.

Mathurānātha is deficient by one *kalā* in both his essential nature (*svarūpa*) and his pastimes (*līlā*) when compared to the Lord of Vṛndāvana; however, in the city of Mathurā and during the Mathurā-līlā, he is complete with all sixteen *kalās*. Likewise, Dvārakānātha is [deficient] in both his essential nature and his pastimes when compared to the Lord of Vṛndāvana.
He is deficient by two *kalās* [in Mathurā],
but in Dvārakā and in the pastimes of Dvārakā, He is complete with all sixteen *kalās*.
Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, Yogamāyā, and likewise the conceivable and inconceivable [energies] are present there.
Mohinī and Kauśalī—these eight are the external powers (śaktis).
Līlā is the very nature of love; she is the one who establishes, the attractor, the uniter, the separator, and the delighter—thus she is the innermost [aspect].
In Vraja, there are sixteen energies of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra;
these eternal ones are indeed the nourishers of His very sweetness.
The great power Hlādinī, who is the most excellent among all powers,
is celebrated as Śrī Rādhikā, whose essential nature is the state of being that very essence.
O sage, at the time of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra’s play,
she beheld Vāsudeva, who was possessed by Him, together with the Lord of the Ocean of Milk.
The power of attraction belonging to Hari should cause [the thread] to go into the intermediate space;
at the end of the play, the power of establishment should place that thread from the body of Kṛṣṇa.
The sole delighter of Nanda, possessing all sixteen digits of perfection,
attains supreme bliss while sporting together with Rādhā.
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Lord, when Kṛṣṇa had gone to the city of Madhu, how did the sentiment of separation arise for Rādhikā toward Vāsudeva? Please dispel this doubt of mine."
Śrī Sadāśiva said:
Śakti is the consort associated with desire; Vāmā is the power of separation;
Hlādinī is the daughter who bestows fame—thus is the triad of Rādhās in Vraja.
"My lord of life, Kṛṣṇa, having left Vṛndāvana,
never goes anywhere else"— this is what the daughter of Kīrtidā knows.
"O son of Brahmā,
they did not realize that the delighter of Nanda had vanished, just as at the beginning of the Rāsa dance."
O sage, when the son of Nanda had disappeared into the glorious Vṛndāvana, Vāsudeva, the Lord of Mathurā, went to Mathurā.
Rādhā, the daughter of Kīrtidā, indeed attained the sentiment known as separation (pravāsa);
therefore, the sages declare that separation is the falling away from union.
"My leader of life has abandoned me and gone to Mathurā"—
thus did the beautiful Rādhā become overwhelmed by the pain of separation.
Having submerged herself in the Yamunā and emerged into the light of Gokula, she reached Goloka,
where she became exquisite with the essence of union.
Kāma and Rādhā, tormented by their separation from Mathurā,
went to Kurukṣetra, being intensely eager for a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
Knowing the state of Nanda’s joy, Uddhava returned to Vraja two months later to console Kīrtidā’s daughter.
O best of sages, when the discourse on the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam had begun, he relished Rādhā, who embodies the meaning of the Bhāgavatam.
Then the glorious son of the lord of Vraja appeared before his very eyes.

Therefore, it should be understood that the departure of the Lord of Dvārakā toward Vṛndāvana, as described in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, was solely for the purpose of restoring Droṇa and others—who had been possessed by the Lord reclining on the Milk Ocean and who had received boons—to their own original abodes.
Such an interpretation of the statements in the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* is to be understood; however, in the *Padmottara-khaṇḍa*, it is said: "On the sandy bank of the Kālindī..."

Regarding the word "ramye" (in the beautiful place), the intended meaning should be understood as follows: out of longing to behold the sweet pastimes of the Lord of Śrī Dvārakā, who is the son of Nanda, they arrived by means of celestial vehicles and dwelt for two months in Śrī Vṛndāvana.
As it is said in the *Śrī Lalita-mādhava* (8.34):
"—never before fully conceptualized," and so forth.
Thus, O Nārada, I have related to you the entire eternal life-story of Hari;
even sinners are liberated by the mere remembrance of him.
Immediately after the service prescribed for the eight periods, the practitioner,
free from sloth, should sequentially recite the mantras, the foremost of which consists of thirty-two syllables.
First one should recite the Great Mantra, and immediately after that, the ten-syllable mantra;
then the mantra of Śrī Rādhikā, as well as the Gāyatrī and the Kāmākī.
Then one should recite the couple-mantra that bestows the site of the *rāsa* dance;
thereafter, one should recite the mantras of the eight female companions (*sakhīs*) in their proper order;
and then, one should recite the individual mantras of the six *mañjarīs* in sequence.
As it is said in the Ādi-purāṇa:

"O Dhanañjaya, those devotees who worship Me alone with the sentiment of being a cowherd girl (gopī-bhāva)—with them, as with those girls, I am pleased; this is the truth, the absolute truth. (RKK 145)
By assuming the dress, ornaments, age, and form of the gopīs,
those who possess devotion attain that very state through the worship of the dust of her feet.
As it is said in the *Ekāmra-purāṇa*:
"Oh, how great is the majesty of the worship of Hari, the Lord of Vṛndāvana!
For there, a man becomes a woman, and a woman becomes equal to the Self. (RKK 147)
And in the *Pādma-purāṇa* (Uttara-khaṇḍa):
"In former times, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
having beheld Rāma there as Hari of the beautiful form, desired to eat [him]."
They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
And the Vedic scriptures, such as the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka and the Vāmana, having served Him in the form of cowherd girls as in former times, indeed manifested in Gokula.
As it was said by the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī:
"That best of men who serves Hari through the path of intense passion (surāga) shall, at that time, attain the very state of a gopī in Vraja by means of that alone. (RKK 151)
In the *Bhakti-tattva-kaumudī*:

"If the contemplation of another [deity] occurs within the body of latent impressions belonging to one [person], then there will indeed be equality between them, just as it was with King Bharata. (RKK 152)
As it is said in the Sanat-kumāra-saṃhitā:
Śrī Nārada said:
"O Goddess, I am blessed and I am graced by you; of this there is no doubt."
For today the eternal play of Hari has been revealed to me.
Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
Having spoken thus and circumambulated her, and being honored by her in return,
O King, Nārada, the best of sages, vanished from sight.
I too have proclaimed all of this in its proper sequence,
by constantly and diligently reciting this unsurpassed pair of mantras.
In former times, this was obtained with great effort from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa by Rudra;
he then spoke it to Nārada, and it has been declared by me as taught by Nārada.
This has been spoken by me to you for the destruction of the fire of saṃsāra;
and this most wonderful secret must be kept hidden by you.
Śrī Ambarīṣa said:
"O Guru, by your direct grace I have become one who has accomplished his purpose,
since that which is the most secret of secrets has been revealed to me by you."
The venerable Sanatkumāra said:
"Having been instructed in these duties, by chanting the mantra day and night, you will before long attain his state of servitude; of this there is no doubt."
"These dharmas" refers to the practice of the eight-fold service;
"mantra" refers to the Yugala-mantra (the mantra of the Divine Couple);
and "service to Them" means the state of servitude or being a maidservant to Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
O King, I too am going to my guru’s abode in Vṛndāvana,
where my guru Sadāśiva resides eternally.
The sequential fruits of mantras consisting of thirty-two syllables and so forth are as stated in the *Pādma*:
"A Vaiṣṇava who constantly recites a mantra of thirty-two syllables accompanied by the sixteen names shall indeed attain the realm of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa. (RKK 161)
And in the Gautamīya Tantra:
"The practitioner of mantra, with a restrained mind, should recite the mantra day and night; he will undoubtedly behold the Lord in the form of a cowherd. (RKK 162)
And in the Gaurī-tantra:
"The practitioner who recites the glorious eight-syllabled mantra of Rādhā, which bestows the perfection of love, shall attain the presence of Rādhā. (RKK 163)
In the Sanat-kumāra-saṃhitā:
"He who recites the Kāma-gāyatrī conjoined with the Kāma-bīja shall attain perfection;
he shall attain love and go to the realm of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (RKK 164)
Having recited these five verses with faith or even without faith, though not repeatedly, one will certainly attain service to Them in Vṛndāvana; of this there is no doubt.
And in the Kiśorī-tantra:
"The practitioner who recites these mantras of the eight companions will quickly attain the place of recreation of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (RKK 166)
In that very place— whoever should constantly recite these mantras of the eight *mañjarīs*,
for him there shall be the perfection of divine love, and he shall attain Śrī Vṛndāvana. (RKK 167)
Immediately after that recollection, the practitioner, whose body has become perfected, should,
while possessing the limbs of a practitioner, recollect the play manifested during the eight times.

The two times—the end of night and the forenoon, as well as the afternoon and the onset of evening—should be understood as consisting of three *ghaṭikās* each; whereas the morning and the evening consist of two *ghaṭikās* each.
It should be known that two *praghaṭika*s each constitute midday and midnight.
During these very occasions, the practitioner should recollect each and every play previously described, at the appropriate time.
Thus ends the manual for the sequence of remembering the eight-fold pastimes of Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, composed by Śrī Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī.
